validated_results.title: Are strict vegetarians protected against prostate cancer?
validated_results.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of 26,346 men reporting a vegan dietary pattern with an incident prostate cancer hazard ratio, so the requested nutritional exposure and incidence outcome are both present and separable.

extraction.comparison_type: Vegan diet compared with nonvegetarian dietary pattern
extraction.population: Male participants of the Adventist Health Study-2

sample_size.excerpt: This study aimed to examine the association between dietary patterns (nonvegetarian, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian, vegan, and semi-vegetarian) and prostate cancer incidence among 26,346 male participants of the Adventist Health Study-2. In this prospective cohort study, cancer cases were identified by matching to cancer registries.

cases.excerpt: In total, 1079 incident prostate cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Vegan diets showed a statistically significant protective association with prostate cancer risk (HR: 0.65; 95% CI: 0.49, 0.85).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Vegan diets showed a statistically significant protective association with prostate cancer risk (HR: 0.65; 95% CI: 0.49, 0.85).

comparison.excerpt: association between dietary patterns (nonvegetarian, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian, vegan, and semi-vegetarian) and prostate cancer incidence

design.excerpt: In this prospective cohort study, cancer cases were identified by matching to cancer registries.

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Around 8% of the study population reported adherence to the vegan diet.

parallel_r3_gate_reasons: important quantitative evidence remains missing or invalid: p_value

validated_results.title: A prospective study of plasma 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration and prostate cancer risk.
validated_results.reason: Nested case-control study within a prospective cohort reports a population-wide association between baseline plasma 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration and incident prostate cancer risk.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile of plasma 25(OH)D (Q4 v. Q1)
extraction.population: Men in the Supplémentation en Vitamines et Minéraux Antioxydants (SU.VI.MAX) cohort

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 129 cases diagnosed within the Supplémentation en Vitamines et Minéraux Antioxydants cohort were included in a nested case-control study and matched to 167 controls (13 years of follow-up).
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 129 + 167 = 296

cases.excerpt: A total of 129 cases diagnosed within the Supplémentation en Vitamines et Minéraux Antioxydants cohort were included in a nested case-control study and matched to 167 controls (13 years of follow-up).

effect_size.excerpt: Higher 25(OH)D concentration was associated with decreased risk of prostate cancer (ORQ4 v. Q1 0·30; 95 % CI 0·12, 0·77; P trend=0·007).

design.excerpt: included in a nested case-control study and matched to 167 controls (13 years of follow-up)

timing.excerpt: In this prospective study, prostate cancer risk was inversely associated with 25(OH)D concentration

exposure_measurement.excerpt: 25-Hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) and PTH concentrations were assessed from baseline plasma samples.

parallel_r3_gate_reasons: important quantitative evidence remains missing or invalid: p_value

validated_results.title: Development and Application of a Lifestyle Score for Prevention of Lethal Prostate Cancer.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Low processed meat intake is only one component of a combined lifestyle/diet score and no processed-meat-specific estimate for prostate cancer is reported.

validated_results.title: Development and Application of a Lifestyle Score for Prevention of Lethal Prostate Cancer.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: High tomato intake is embedded in a multi-component lifestyle and diet-only score with no tomato-specific prostate cancer estimate reported.

validated_results.title: Dietary tocopherols inhibit PhIP-induced prostate carcinogenesis in CYP1A-humanized mice.
validated_results.reason: The study exclusively tests dietary tocopherols in CYP1A-humanized mice with chemically induced prostatic lesions, providing no human data.

validated_results.title: Associations between circulating carotenoids, genomic instability and the risk of high-grade prostate cancer.
validated_results.reason: Circulating β-carotene is compared across men already diagnosed with prostate cancer for the outcome of high-grade (Gleason) disease and genomic instability, not prostate cancer incidence.

validated_results.title: Associations between circulating carotenoids, genomic instability and the risk of high-grade prostate cancer.
validated_results.reason: Plasma lycopene is related to tumour grade and genomic instability among prostatectomy patients, so no incident prostate cancer endpoint is available.

validated_results.title: Associations between circulating carotenoids, genomic instability and the risk of high-grade prostate cancer.
validated_results.reason: No tomato food intake was assessed; the study measured circulating carotenoid concentrations only.

validated_results.title: Cancer chemoprevention research with selenium in the post-SELECT era: Promises and challenges.
validated_results.reason: This is a narrative review and commentary on selenium chemoprevention trials rather than an original human study.

validated_results.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Consumption and Prostate Cancer: A Review of Exposure Measures and Results of Epidemiological Studies.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the American College of Nutrition
validated_results.reason: The article is a review synthesising 36 previously published epidemiological studies of omega-3 intake and prostate cancer.

validated_results.title: Prostate cancer and glutathione S-transferase deletions.
validated_results.reason: The exposure studied is GSTM1/GSTT1 gene deletion polymorphism, not nutritional glutathione intake or status.
